setupSteps: Mat and space. Lay the mat on a flat, non-slip floor. Keep at least 2 m of clear floor so the top arm can sweep out.
Clothes. Fitted top and track pants or leggings so the shoulders and hips show on camera. Remove a watch or loose bangles that dig into the floor.

Open book (A). Lie on one side. Pillow or folded towel under the head if the neck feels tilted. Bend hips and knees to about 90 degrees (est.), thighs forward of the body, knees and feet stacked. Arms straight out in front at shoulder height, palms together.
Knee wedge (optional but helpful). A cushion or folded towel between the knees reminds you to keep the knees stacked and the pelvis from rolling back.
Quadruped (B). Hands under shoulders, knees under hips (hips and knees at about 90 degrees, est.). Fold a towel under knees and wrists if the floor is hard.

Doorway (C). Stand in a doorway with one forearm or hand on the frame, upper arm out to the side at about shoulder height (est. 80–100 degrees from the body), elbow bent about 90 degrees (est.). One foot a half step forward for balance.
Camera. For the quadruped rotation: phone on the floor or a low stool at mat height, 2 m in front of you (head end), landscape, so both shoulders, both elbows and hips are in frame (see section 11).

steps.title: Lie on your side and stack the knees
steps.action: lie on one side, hips and knees bent about 90 degrees, knees and feet stacked, arms straight ahead with palms together.
steps.feel: supported, hips heavy on the mat.
steps.visualCheck: front view (from the feet or above), knees stacked and level; side view, thighs forward, spine long.

steps.title: Lock the pelvis and knees
steps.action: press the top knee down onto the bottom knee (or the cushion) and keep the lower back long, not arched.
steps.feel: a light steadiness in the glutes and deep belly; lower back quiet.
steps.visualCheck: top knee stays on the bottom knee through the whole move.

steps.title: Lift and lead with the hand
steps.action: lift the top arm just off the other hand and let your eyes follow it.
steps.feel: a mild turning feeling in the mid-back.
steps.visualCheck: head turns with the hand, neck stays long, not craned.

steps.title: Open the book
steps.action: slowly rotate the chest and open the top arm out and back toward the floor behind you, going only as far as the knees stay stacked.
steps.feel: stretch across the front of the chest and shoulder, gentle turn between the shoulder blades; no pinch in the low back or shoulder.
steps.breathing: breathe out slowly as you open.
steps.visualCheck: the opening comes from the ribcage turning, not from the knees falling away or the back arching.

steps.title: Pause at your comfortable end range
steps.action: stop where it feels like a mild-to-moderate stretch; do not force the arm to touch the floor. Let the shoulder blade settle.
steps.feel: light effort 3–4/10 on the ACSM 0–10 effort scale (= Borg 9–11 on the 6–20 scale).
steps.breathing: one slow breath in and out.
steps.visualCheck: chest turned toward the ceiling, top knee still on the bottom knee.

steps.title: Close the book
steps.action: breathe in and sweep the arm back to meet the other hand, leading with the hand and letting the chest turn back.
steps.visualCheck: palms touching again, no jerk at the end.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.action: repeat steps 3 to 6 for 8 slow reps (see section 7), then turn over and do the other side.
steps.feel: more freedom each rep, never pain.
steps.breathing: out on opening, in on closing.
steps.visualCheck: same range each rep, knees stacked.

steps.title: Come onto hands and knees
steps.action: hands under shoulders, knees under hips, spine neutral, eyes on the floor.
steps.feel: weight even across hands and knees.
steps.visualCheck: side view, back flat like a table; front view, shoulders level.

steps.title: Place one hand behind the head
steps.action: slide one hand behind the head with the fingertips lightly touching; the other arm stays straight under the shoulder.
steps.visualCheck: supporting elbow nearly straight (not locked), elbow of the other arm pointing out to the side.

steps.title: Rock the hips slightly back (optional lock)
steps.action: sit the hips back a hand's width toward the heels to lock the low back, as one physio source teaches.
steps.feel: the low back "switched off", the movement will come from the mid-back.
steps.visualCheck: hips stay still for the rest of the set.

steps.title: Rotate down
steps.action: bring the elbow of the hand behind your head down toward the opposite elbow, turning the chest to the floor.
steps.feel: a gentle rounding and turning in the mid-back.
steps.visualCheck: front view, elbow below the shoulder line.

steps.title: Rotate up and open
steps.action: turn the chest to the side and lift that elbow toward the ceiling, following it with your eyes, as far as is comfortable; keep the hips level.
steps.feel: chest opening, mid-back turning, light work between the shoulder blades.
steps.visualCheck: front view, elbow level with or above the shoulder; hips have not shifted sideways.

steps.title: Return and repeat
steps.action: lower the elbow back under the body in a slow controlled path. 6 to 8 reps, then switch hands.
steps.breathing: out on lowering, in on opening (or whichever feels natural; never hold the breath).
steps.visualCheck: no side-bending of the neck, no rocking of the hips.

steps.title: Take the position
steps.action: stand in a doorway, forearm or hand on the frame at about shoulder height, elbow bent about 90 degrees, one foot half a step forward.
steps.visualCheck: front view, elbow roughly at shoulder height; side view, standing tall.

steps.title: Turn away gently
steps.action: slowly turn the chest and body away from the frame until a mild stretch appears across the front of the chest. Do not lean forward so far that the low back arches.
steps.feel: a mild-to-moderate pull in the chest and front shoulder, never sharp, never numbness or tingling in the arm or hand.
steps.breathing: slow, easy breathing; never hold it.
steps.visualCheck: ribs stay down, shoulders not shrugged.

steps.title: Release and switch
steps.action: turn back and lower the arm slowly; repeat on the other arm. 2 rounds per side.
steps.visualCheck: no sudden drop of the arm.

commonMistakes.title: Twisting from the low back, with the knees falling away or the pelvis rolling
commonMistakes.text: Twisting from the low back, with the knees falling away or the pelvis rolling. The low back is not built to rotate much, and the thoracic spine gets none of the work. Fix: stack the knees (cushion between them) and cue "ribs turn, hips stay".

commonMistakes.title: Throwing the arm back with momentum
commonMistakes.text: Throwing the arm back with momentum. Range comes from the arm swinging, not the spine turning, and the shoulder can be stressed. Fix: slow 3-second opens, eyes on the hand, stop at the first comfortable resistance.

commonMistakes.title: Chasing the floor with the arm
commonMistakes.text: Chasing the floor with the arm. Forcing the arm to touch the mat strains the shoulder and the front of the chest. Fix: work to a mild stretch; the end range will grow over weeks.

commonMistakes.title: Side-bending the trunk instead of rotating (quadruped)
commonMistakes.text: Side-bending the trunk instead of rotating (quadruped). The move becomes a lean, not a turn. Fix: keep both shoulders at the same distance from the floor and turn the chest, not the shoulder line toward the hip.

commonMistakes.title: Pressing or pulling on the head
commonMistakes.text: Pressing or pulling on the head. Neck strain. Fix: fingertips only on the head, or rest the hand on the upper back.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Raises tension and, in people with high blood pressure, adds strain. Fix: breathe out on opening, breathe normally through holds.

commonMistakes.title: Over-arching the low back in the doorway stretch
commonMistakes.text: Over-arching the low back in the doorway stretch. Leaning in to feel more chest stretch puts the work in the low back. Fix: ribs down, belly lightly drawn in, smaller range.

commonMistakes.title: Bouncing into the chest stretch
commonMistakes.text: Bouncing into the chest stretch. Bouncing is called out as a common mistake in physio libraries. Fix: move slowly in and out, hold still.

commonMistakes.title: Skipping the stronger hand or side
commonMistakes.text: Skipping the stronger hand or side. People stretch only the tight side. Fix: do both sides and note differences (see "film yourself").

safetyNotes: Lower back: keep the pelvis and knees still, move only within a comfortable range, and stop if back pain increases or leg symptoms start. NHS leaflets say keep moving and avoid long rest, but do not continue exercises that significantly increase pain.

Osteoporosis or bone thinning: use the slow side-lying version with small range, no forced or fast twisting, no pushing the arm to the floor. The International Osteoporosis Foundation advises avoiding powerful twisting movements of the trunk, and the UK consensus statement (BJSM 2022) advises avoiding postures with a high degree of spinal flexion and recommends extension exercises. With a known spine fracture, ask a doctor or physio first.

Shoulder problems: doorway chest stretch is listed as unsuitable with acute shoulder impingement, a recent rotator cuff injury or chronic shoulder instability (a physio exercise library), so skip it and use lighter versions (elbow lower, smaller turn). Stop if there is pinching, numbness, tingling or pins and needles in the arm or hand.
Neck: keep the neck long; do not force the head round; stop with neck pain or arm tingling.
Knees or wrists: pad under the knees and wrists, or use the side-lying or standing versions.

Pregnancy: avoid lying flat on the back for long periods, especially after 16 weeks (Tommy's, citing NICE; the earlier RCOG advice was based on expert opinion per a 2019 BJSM review), so do the seated or quadruped version and keep the open arm in a modest range.
Recent surgery (chest, spine, abdomen): wait for the surgeon or physio before twisting or stretching the chest wall.
Asthma: keep the reliever inhaler nearby; stop if you wheeze or feel breathless.
Spine conditions: scoliosis, a herniated disc or a spinal fracture mean checking with your doctor before thread the needle (Livestrong).

Stop immediately if you feel: sharp or pinching pain in the back, shoulder or neck; pain, tingling or numbness down an arm or leg; chest pain, dizziness or breathlessness; new bladder or bowel changes with back pain (an NHS leaflet lists these as red flags).
Gym etiquette: use the stretching area or a mat out of walkways; wipe the mat after use.

Open book dose: 10 reps per side (Bone Coach), 30 s to 1 min per side (osteopath), 5–10 reps (ACE). We chose 8 slow reps per side, 2 rounds.
Doorway hold time: 15 s × 3 (handouts), 30–60 s (Fit&Well), 10–30 s (ACSM). We chose 20–30 s × 2 per side.
Quadruped lock: some sources start with the hips rocked back to lock the low back; others keep a neutral spine with a braced core. We offer the rock-back as an optional cue.

Hand placement: behind the head (most common), behind the lower back or upper back (some sources). We use behind the head with light fingertips, or on the upper back if the shoulder or neck complains.

Osteoporosis and rotation: the UK consensus warns against high spinal flexion and recommends extension work; the IOF advises avoiding powerful trunk twisting; Bone Coach teaches a gentle open book. We chose "modify": slow, small range, no forced twisting, and ask a doctor with a known spine fracture.

Pregnancy: older RCOG advice about avoiding lying on the back after 16 weeks was expert opinion; UK parenting and charity pages still repeat it. We chose the cautious "avoid lying flat on the back" and offer seated or quadruped.
Evidence strength: thoracic mobility exercise has low-quality evidence and only small trials; we state benefits as likely, not proven.
